HTECH-CTX-G2.title: Dockhand design summary v1.3 (candidate project)
HTECH-CTX-G2.text:
DOCKHAND - Design Summary (v1.3)
Author: Tobias Venkataraman | Larkspur Freight, Platform Backend | Last updated: 2024-11-18
Status: in production since June 2024

1. Purpose
Dockhand moves shipment status events (picked up, in transit, delayed, delivered, exception) from the services that record them into Kafka, so that billing, the customer portal and the carrier-settlement services from Project Tern can react without polling the database. Volume is about 2.3 million events per day on average, with a morning peak of roughly 410 events per second between 07:30 and 09:00 Eastern.

2. Why an outbox
Before Dockhand, services wrote to PostgreSQL and then published to Kafka in the same request. When the publish failed after the commit, the event was lost; when the commit failed after the publish, consumers saw an event for a change that never happened. Dockhand uses a transactional outbox: the service writes the business row and an outbox row in the same PostgreSQL transaction. Nothing is published inside the request.

3. Components
- outbox_events table: one row per event (event_id UUID, shipment_id, event_type, payload JSONB, created_at, published_at). Partitioned by day; partitions older than 72 hours are dropped by a scheduled job, which is cheaper than DELETE plus vacuum.
- Relay: a Go service that polls unpublished rows every 250 ms in batches of up to 500, ordered by created_at, publishes them, then sets published_at. Two relay instances run, but only one is active at a time: the active one holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock. If it dies, the standby acquires the lock; failover has taken up to 30 seconds in drills.
- Topic shipment-status.v2: 24 partitions, keyed by shipment_id, replication factor 3, producer acks=all.
- Consumers: each consumer records processed event_id values in a dedupe table (processed_events) inside the same transaction as its own side effects. Entries are kept for 7 days.
- Dead-letter topic shipment-status.dlq: a message goes there after 5 failed attempts with exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds.

4. Delivery guarantees
Dockhand is at-least-once, not exactly-once. The relay can publish a batch and crash before it sets published_at; on restart that batch is published again. Duplicates are expected and are removed by the consumer-side dedupe on event_id. Ordering is guaranteed per shipment only (same key, same partition). There is no ordering across shipments.

5. Service levels
Target: p99 time from outbox commit to consumer receipt under 4 seconds. Measured in October 2024: p50 0.6 s, p99 2.9 s, excluding relay failovers.

6. Alternatives considered
- Debezium change data capture: rejected for v1 because the platform team did not run Kafka Connect yet, and we did not want to own a Connect cluster for one pipeline. Revisit in 2025.
- Publishing directly from the request with retries: rejected; it cannot close the gap between commit and publish.
- SQS FIFO: rejected because the billing and settlement teams already consumed from Kafka, and FIFO throughput limits per message group would have needed careful sharding.

7. Known limitations
- The single active relay is a throughput ceiling; load tests showed it saturates near 3,000 events per second.
- JSON payloads carry a schema_version field, but there is no schema registry; breaking changes are coordinated by hand.
- The dedupe window is 7 days, so replaying older messages from the DLQ requires a manual override flag.

8. Open questions
- Whether to move the relay to logical replication once Kafka Connect exists.
- Whether 24 partitions is enough if the Tern consumers need more parallelism.

HTECH-CTX-G1.title: Tallowmarket Go coding session pre-read: Escrow Hold Overlap
HTECH-CTX-G1.text:
TALLOWMARKET - GO CODING SESSION PRE-READ
Problem: Escrow Hold Overlap (version 2)

Background
When a restaurant places an order, Tallowmarket places an escrow hold on the funds until the grower confirms delivery. Our Risk team wants to know how many holds are open at the same time, because the banking partner charges a fee tier based on the peak number of simultaneous holds in a day.

Part A (required)
You are given n holds. Each hold has an id, a start minute and an end minute. A hold covers the half-open interval [start, end): it is active at minute start and no longer active at minute end. Two holds that touch (one ends at 40, the other starts at 40) do not overlap.
Return two integers: the maximum number of holds active at the same instant, and the earliest instant at which that maximum is reached. If n is 0, return "0 -1".

Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 200,000
- 0 <= start < end <= 1,000,000,000 (integers, minutes since the start of the settlement epoch)
- Holds are NOT sorted. Ids are unique strings of up to 12 characters.
- Target: O(n log n) time. Your solution runs with a 2 second limit and 256 MB of memory.

Example 1
Input:
H1 10 50
H2 20 40
H3 40 70
H4 45 60
H5 70 90
Output: 3 45
Explanation: at minute 45, H1, H3 and H4 are active. At minute 40, H2 has already ended, so only H1 and H3 are active there.

Example 2
Input:
H1 5 15
H2 15 25
H3 25 35
Output: 1 5

Example 3
Input: (no holds)
Output: 0 -1

Part B (required)
Each hold also carries amount_cents, a positive integer up to 50,000,000. Return the maximum total amount_cents held at the same instant and the earliest instant it is reached. Use a 64-bit integer; the sum can exceed 2^31.

Example 4
Input:
H1 0 30 5000
H2 10 20 9000
H3 20 40 7000
Output: 14000 10
Explanation: during [10, 20) H1 and H2 are both held, 14000 in total. At minute 20, H2 ends and H3 starts, so the total drops to H1 + H3 = 12000.

Part C (discussion only, no code)
Holds will eventually arrive as a stream from Kafka, up to 50,000 inserts per second at peak, and a hold may also be cancelled before its end minute. Describe how you would keep the Part A answer current after each insert or cancel. We care about the data structure and its complexity, not a full implementation.

What we look at
- Correct handling of touching intervals. This is the most common mistake we see.
- Tie-breaking: when the maximum is reached more than once, report the earliest instant.
- Clear naming and small functions. Standard library only; no third-party packages.
- A few table-driven tests.

Please do not share this problem publicly. Questions about the statement can be raised with the session interviewer at the start of the call.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Alright, let's get going. Why does quicksort go quadratic in the worst case, and how do real implementations avoid that?
conversation: INTERVIEWER: Sorry, I'm a couple minutes late, the parking garage by our office was full again.
USER (spoken): No worries at all. Traffic was rough on my side this morning too.
INTERVIEWER: Ha, yeah. Did you end up watching the game on Saturday?
USER (spoken): Only the second half, it was a close one.
items.answer:
Quicksort goes quadratic when the pivot splits the array as unevenly as possible, so each partition peels off just one element and you get n levels of recursion, each doing O(n) work. That happens with a sorted or reverse-sorted input under a naive first-or-last-element pivot, since every element lands on one side.

Real implementations avoid it in a few ways. They pick the pivot more carefully, like median-of-three or a random pivot, so a bad split is unlikely rather than guaranteed. Many also switch to insertion sort on small subarrays and use introsort, which tracks recursion depth and falls back to heapsort if it gets too deep, giving an O(n log n) worst-case guarantee.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Let's start easy. What's the actual difference between a process and a thread?
items.answer: A process is an independent program with its own address space, so processes are isolated from each other. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process, and threads in the same process share that memory and its resources. That sharing makes threads cheaper to create and switch between, but it also means one thread's bad write can corrupt the others.

What I did afterward was write the team's first incident runbooks, 14 of them, so the next person on call had a documented path instead of starting from scratch.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Okay, design question. Say we run managed Postgres for thousands of customers on our own bare metal. Each database has one primary and two replicas. Design automatic failover: how you detect the primary is dead, how you pick the new one, how clients find it, and how you avoid losing acknowledged writes.
items.answer: I'd run a consensus layer, something like etcd or Patroni, as the source of truth for who's primary, rather than trusting the nodes to agree among themselves. Each primary streams WAL to both replicas, and the leader key is held with a lease that has to be renewed. If the primary can't renew, the lease expires and the consensus layer promotes the replica with the most advanced WAL, so we don't lose acknowledged writes. Clients never hardcode an address, they go through a proxy or a virtual IP that follows the leader key. And I'd fence the old primary hard before promotion, so it can't come back and accept writes.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: On your resume you've got the rate quote API going from 820 to 190 milliseconds at p95. Say right after that launch p95 looks great but p99 gets worse and you see periodic spikes. Given how you built the cache, what's your first guess, how would you confirm it, and what would you change?
items.answer:
My first guess is cache stampede on the hot lanes. With a 90-second TTL keyed by lane ID, the popular keys all expire together, so a burst of requests misses at once and hits Postgres with the batched loader, which shows up as p99 spikes while p95 stays flat.

To confirm, I'd graph cache hit ratio and Postgres query rate against the spike timestamps, and check whether the misses cluster on a few lane IDs. If they do, I'd add jitter to the TTL and single-flight the loader so only one request per key refills it.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Tell me about Dockhand. Roughly how many events a day was it handling, and why did you go with Kafka for it?
items.answer:
Dockhand is a Kafka event pipeline I designed at Larkspur Freight that processes about **2.3 million shipment status events per day**. The core problem was that shipment status updates were being written straight into the database, and we needed to avoid duplicate writes, so I used a **transactional outbox table** to make the publish reliable. Kafka gave us a durable, ordered log we could replay from, which fit the volume and the need to fan those events out to downstream consumers without hammering Postgres.

On why Kafka specifically over something simpler: the evidence I have covers the design and the outbox, but it doesn't spell out the full reasoning behind the choice, so I'd frame that as the tradeoffs I weighed rather than a documented decision.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Heap versus BST?
items.answer:
A heap is optimized for one thing: getting the min or max in O(1) time, with insert and extract in O(log n). It's a partially ordered structure, so a parent is only guaranteed to compare correctly against its children, not across the whole tree. A BST keeps a full ordering, so you can search, find predecessors and successors, and do an in-order traversal to get sorted output, all in O(log n) when balanced.

So the choice comes down to what you need. If it's a priority queue, top-k, or a streaming median, a heap is the right tool. If you need ordered lookups, range queries, or sorted iteration, a BST, or a balanced variant like a red-black or AVL tree, is what you want.

items.question: Why not Debezium?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): So, Dockhand. The outbox means you never publish the same event twice, right? Walk me through how the relay guarantees that.

NATIVELY: No, not exactly. Dockhand is at-least-once, not exactly-once. The relay polls unpublished rows every 250 ms in batches of up to 500, ordered by created_at, publishes them, then sets published_at. If it crashes after publishing but before setting published_at, that batch gets published again on restart, so duplicates are expected. What removes them is consumer-side dedupe: each consumer records processed event_id values in a processed_events table inside the same transaction as its own side effects, and those entries are kept for 7 days. So the guarantee is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers, not a relay that never publishes twice.
items.answer: We did look at Debezium. We rejected it for v1 because the platform team didn't run Kafka Connect yet, and we didn't want to own a Connect cluster just for one pipeline. The outbox relay was something we could build and operate ourselves. It's on the list to revisit in 2025, once Connect exists.

items.question: Postgres runs at serializable by default, right? So which anomalies can you still hit?
items.answer: Actually, Postgres defaults to read committed, not serializable. Serializable is opt-in per transaction, and even then it's SSI, so you can still get serialization failures that abort and need retry. What it rules out is the classic anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, and write skew.

items.question: What about space?
conversation: INTERVIEWER: Okay, so you wrote Fibonacci top-down, plain recursion with a hash map as the memo.
USER (spoken): Right, and each value from zero to n gets computed once, so time is linear.

items.answer: Space is O(n) for the memo table, since we store one entry per value from zero to n. The recursion stack adds O(n) depth too, so overall it's O(n) space. If we wanted to cut that, we could go bottom-up and keep just the last two values, which drops it to O(1).

items.answer:
The evidence doesn't record a specific disagreement, so I'd answer from how I actually handle it, using Project Tern as the real anchor. Something like:

"On Project Tern, the carrier-settlement rewrite, the working group split on how to sequence the migration off the Rails monolith. I wrote up the tradeoffs in a design doc, we walked through the failure modes together, and settled it on the evidence rather than who felt strongest. What I care about is disagreeing on the technical merits, then committing fully once we decide. I'd rather lose the argument early than have a design nobody believes in."

items.question: This is supposed to return the first index where a[i] >= target, but it hangs on some inputs. lo, hi := 0, len(a)-1; for lo < hi { mid := (lo + hi) / 2; if a[mid] < target { lo = mid } else { hi = mid - 1 } }; return lo. What's wrong with it?
items.answer: Two bugs. When `a[mid] < target` you set `lo = mid`, so lo never advances past mid and the loop spins forever. And `hi = mid - 1` can skip the answer. Use `lo = mid + 1` and `hi = mid`, with `hi := len(a)`.

items.question: Have you actually run something like this for real, or is this from reading?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Okay, design question. Say we run managed Postgres for thousands of customers on our own bare metal. Each database has one primary and two replicas. Design automatic failover: how you detect the primary is dead, how you pick the new one, how clients find it, and how you avoid losing acknowledged writes.

NATIVELY: I'd run a consensus layer, something like etcd or Patroni, as the source of truth for who's primary, rather than trusting the nodes to agree among themselves. Each primary streams WAL to both replicas, and the leader key is held with a lease that has to be renewed. If the primary can't renew, the lease expires and the consensus layer promotes the replica with the most advanced WAL, so we don't lose acknowledged writes. Clients never hardcode an address, they go through a proxy or a virtual IP that follows the leader key. And I'd fence the old primary hard before promotion, so it can't come back and accept writes.

NATIVELY: Split brain is exactly what the fencing and the lease are there to prevent. The consensus layer only ever has one leader key, so only one node can be primary at a time. If the old primary is partitioned and can't renew its lease, it loses the key, and before the new one is promoted I fence the old one hard, so even if it's still up it can't accept writes. The risk window is a primary that's alive but cut off from the consensus layer, and the lease expiry plus fencing closes that.
items.answer: I've run pieces of this for real. I've done on-call and game days on GKE, and I've built the observability around it, but I haven't personally owned a Postgres failover at that scale. The consensus and fencing design is from reading and from how I'd approach it.

items.question: Here's the problem. You get an array of integers, which can be negative, and a target k. Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray that sums to exactly k. Start with brute force, then give me the optimal approach, then the time and space, and then tell me whether a sliding window would work here and why or why not.
items.answer:
Brute force: for every start index, extend the end index and keep a running sum, checking each subarray against k. It's correct because it literally examines every contiguous subarray, so the longest match can't be missed. That's O(n²) time and O(1) space, and it's slow because it redoes the same additions over and over.

The optimal approach is a prefix-sum hash map. Keep a running sum as you scan, and store the earliest index where each prefix sum first appeared. At each position, if running sum minus k is a prefix sum you've seen, the subarray between that earlier index and here sums to k, so you take its length. Store each prefix sum only the first time you see it, since the earliest index gives the longest subarray. That's **O(n) time** and **O(n) space**.

A sliding window does not work here, and the reason is the negatives. The window technique relies on the sum moving monotonically as you grow or shrink the window, so you know when to expand and when to contract. With negative numbers, adding an element can decrease the sum and removing one can increase it, so that monotonic assumption breaks and you can't decide the window's direction. Sliding window only works when all values are non-negative.

items.question: Simpler please.
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): they want an LRU cache in Go with O(1) get and put, and I can't use container/list. write it
items.answer: Sure. The idea is a map from key to node, plus a hand-rolled doubly linked list where the front is most recent and the back is least recent. Get looks up the map, moves the node to the front, returns its value. Put updates in place if the key exists, otherwise adds to the front and evicts the tail when over capacity. Both are O(1) because the map gives the node and the list moves it in constant time.

items.question: Okay, you've had the escrow holds problem for a few minutes. Before you write any code, tell me how you'd get the max number of overlapping holds and the first time it happens.
items.answer: I'd sweep the endpoints. Turn each hold into two events: a start at `start` with +1, and an end at `end` with -1. Sort all events by minute, and for ties process the -1 before the +1, so a hold ending at 40 is gone before one starting at 40 counts. Then walk the sorted events keeping a running count, track the max, and record the minute the first time the count hits a new max. That gives the peak and the earliest instant it occurs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space. For Part B I'd carry the amount in the event instead of +1/-1 and track the running sum the same way.

items.question: he wants a double entry ledger schema in postgres. core tables plus the constraints that keep it balanced
items.answer:
Two core tables: **accounts** with an id, name, and type, and **entries** with an id, a reference to the transaction, the account, and an amount. Then a **journal** or transaction table groups entries that must balance.

The balance constraint is the tricky part. A simple check per row won't work, so you enforce it with a deferred constraint trigger that sums the entries per transaction and rejects the commit if the total isn't zero.

items.question: You partitioned that big events table by month. How did you keep event IDs unique across the partitions, and what happened to queries that didn't filter on time?
items.answer: The load_events table was partitioned by month in PostgreSQL, and the event ID stayed the primary key, so uniqueness held across partitions. Queries that didn't filter on time had to scan every partition, so I made sure the hot paths always carried a time predicate.
